content_voiceover: This slide shows a real DDAVP challenge test, used to diagnose type 1C VWD, the enhanced clearance variant. Look at the numbers, before infusion, factor VIII is 58.6%, VWF antigen 39.4%, VWF activity 26.6%, all low but not dramatically so. One hour after DDAVP, everything spikes appropriately, factor VIII to 375%, VWF antigen to 211%, VWF activity to 171%, confirming the patient can actually release VWF from endothelial stores, so DDAVP responsiveness is intact. But by four hours, levels have crashed back down, factor VIII to 128%, VWF antigen to 126%, VWF activity to 96%. Calculate the percent drop from peak to four hours for VWF antigen, that's roughly a 40% decrease, well above the 30% threshold that defines type 1C. The mechanism is accelerated clearance of VWF from plasma, not a synthesis or secretion problem. This is a high-yield distinction because type 1C patients need more frequent DDAVP dosing or tranexamic acid coverage since the boost doesn't last.
keypoints: Type 1C VWD = enhanced VWF clearance, not decreased synthesis
Diagnostic: >30% decrease from peak VWF level at 4-hr post-DDAVP
Normal 1-hr rise (DDAVP responsive) but rapid 4-hr fall
Clinical implication: shorter DDAVP effect, may need repeat dosing/TXA
keypoint_voiceover: Type 1C VWD is diagnosed by the DDAVP challenge test, drawing levels pre-infusion, at one hour, and at four hours. The one-hour level rises normally, showing intact release, but by four hours VWF has dropped over 30% from its peak, confirming accelerated clearance rather than a secretion defect. This matters clinically because the hemostatic benefit of DDAVP is short-lived, so these patients often need more frequent dosing or adjunct tranexamic acid.
